moments.title: Building the tunnel and crib
moments.text: To draw clean water far from the sewage flowing out of the river, city engineer Ellis Chesbrough designed a tunnel under the lake bed reaching two miles out into Lake Michigan, ending at an intake called the Two-Mile Crib.

moments.title: Lake water reaches the city
moments.text: With the tunnel and crib finished, the first water from the new intake flowed into Chicago.

moments.title: A pumping station on shore
moments.text: The tunnel's shore end connected to a new pumping station on Chicago Ave, completed in 1869 along with the Water Tower.

moments.title: A new crib takes over
moments.text: The Carter H. Harrison Crib replaced the Two-Mile Crib, and in 1935 the William E. Dever Crib was built beside it.

moments.title: The original crib is torn down
moments.text: The old Two-Mile Tunnel and Two-Mile Crib were closed and demolished.

moments.title: Today: later cribs offshore
moments.text: The 1867 crib is gone, but later water cribs still stand offshore and can be seen from the lakefront. Location approximate.

checked.notes: Chesbrough's two-mile tunnel and crib; first water Mar 25, 1867 (Wikipedia, Linda Hall Library). Correction: the Two-Mile Crib no longer stands. Wikipedia says the tunnel and crib were closed and demolished in 1936, after the Carter H. Harrison Crib replaced it in 1900; the Dever Crib was built beside Harrison in 1935. 'Today' was changed accordingly. Crib built 1865 (Wikipedia) or 1866 (Lighthouse Friends). Pumping station completed 1869 per a Chicago history blog.
